title: Waste factor
summary: The number you multiply the clean quantity by to know how much to buy as purchased.

what: The waste factor is the number you multiply a clean quantity by to know how much to buy as purchased. It also turns an as-purchased price into its equivalent clean price.
It's best to work it out from the trim waste %, because you'll need that percentage for many other calculations.
formula: Another way: Factor = gross weight ÷ net weight

variables.name: Trim waste %
variables.description: How much of the purchased product is lost when cleaning it.

variables.name: 100 − trim waste %
variables.description: The usable part: what is left clean from every 100 you buy.

variables.name: Waste factor
variables.description: How many times more you must buy as purchased compared with what you need clean.

steps: Take the trim waste % of the raw material.
Work out the usable part: 100 − trim waste %.
Divide the trim waste % by the usable part.

examples.title: Whole salmon
paragraphs: Whole salmon has 25% trim waste (head, bones and skin), so 75% is usable.
For every kilo of clean fillet you need, you have to buy 1.333 kg of whole salmon.

notes.text: With 25% trim waste the factor is not 1.25. If you only add 25%, the extra you bought also loses 25% when trimmed: it is "the waste of the waste", and it never adds up.
Both formulas give the same result. Any small difference comes from rounding decimals.
A factor of 1 means there's no trim: the product is used exactly as purchased.

waste-percentage.label: Trim waste %
waste-percentage.hint: If you don't know it, work it out with the trim waste % formula.
